text: A leaked credential is rarely administrator-level on its own. What makes it dangerous is a specific, well-documented permission combination that lets a low-privilege identity grant itself more access. Both AWS and Azure have their own catalogued versions of this problem, and they follow the exact same underlying logic: find the one action that lets you hand yourself more permission, and use it.

Security researchers have mapped out roughly twenty specific AWS IAM privilege-escalation methods. iam:CreatePolicyVersion lets you set a new default version of a policy you can already edit, rewriting your own effective permissions. iam:PassRole combined with ec2:RunInstances lets you launch an instance, attach a far more privileged role to it, and inherit that role through the instance metadata service. iam:AddUserToGroup is simpler still — add yourself to a group that already has broad permissions attached, and you inherit them instantly.

The shape to watch for in a policy review is PassRole and RunInstances granted together, scoped to a wildcard resource. That combination isn't inherently malicious — plenty of automation legitimately needs it — but unscoped, it's a textbook escalation primitive, and it needs a documented reason to exist rather than a shrug.

Azure's version depends on a single control-plane action: Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write. Both Owner and User Access Administrator include it, and holding it means an identity can assign itself, or anything it controls, a broader role. Separately, Application Administrator can add a brand-new client secret to an existing app registration it didn't create — including one already granted high-privilege Microsoft Graph permissions by someone else — which is a well-documented way to authenticate as a far more powerful identity.

The good news is both platforms ship purpose-built detections. GuardDuty raises named finding types like PrivilegeEscalation:IAMUser/AdministrativePermissions when these IAM patterns get exercised, and in raw CloudTrail you can alert directly on CreatePolicyVersion, AttachUserPolicy, and AddUserToGroup calls from identities that don't normally touch IAM. In Azure, Identity Protection's risk detections — impossible travel, unfamiliar sign-in properties — often fire even earlier, on the sign-in itself, before the escalation attempt ever happens.

Once you can name the specific permission or action behind an escalation attempt, you're ready to go prove it happened. Next, we turn to CloudTrail and the Azure Activity Log as the actual forensic source of truth — how to read the fields that matter and reconstruct exactly what an attacker did, in what order.
